lines: Afternoon. Fine weather for it, if it holds. It usually holds till about nine.
You'll hear the bell at nine, from the School up north. I'm indoors by then, with everything shut up. I've never been out to hear what comes after it.
If you pass a barn with a card on its doors, leave it be. Most have one now. I put one on mine myself, and I couldn't tell you why.
Keep to the road once the lamps are lit. Things come out of the rough ground after dark. They don't come onto the road, mostly. They stand at the edge of it.
The crows have taken to following people instead of the plough. They come along the fence with you as far as the last post and turn back there. Every time, the last post.
Hello, love. You're not from round here. Nobody walks the roads now unless they have to.
We lock the door at nine. You'd be welcome, but we lock it at nine. Everybody along here does.
The children aren't allowed out on the road after tea. I couldn't tell you why. My mother was the same with me.
Have you noticed the lamps come on earlier than they did? I have. I put the kettle on by them, and it's been earlier every week since March.
Making for Castle? Keep to the road and you'll be there before the lamps. Don't cut across. The fields are bigger than they look.
You'll hear the School's bell at nine. It's rung every night I can remember, and nobody's taught up there since I was a boy.
The lamps are lit at dusk and counted at ten. I counted them for years. It never came to the same number twice, and I'm careful.
I've stood about here most days for forty years. The road used to go somewhere else.

country_woman.speaker: A Woman in a Brown Coat

lines: Has the bell been going early for you? I thought it was me. My sister says it's gone before nine twice this week.
I don't let the children past the garden after tea. They used to argue about it. They've stopped arguing, and I don't like that either.
I'm only waiting for my husband. He went to see a man about a cart this morning. He said dinner time, and I've kept it hot twice.
Walking to Castle? Keep to the road once the lamps are lit. Things come up to the edge of it after dark. They don't come onto it, as a rule.
Mind the stumps. I've not had them out yet. I cut on this side of the wood. Nobody cuts the other side, and it doesn't grow.
I'm off home well before the bell. It carries in a wood. You'd swear it was the next clearing over.
There's something in the trees after dark, bigger than a fox. I've never seen it. I've seen where it's lain down, and it lies down facing the road.
I leave the axe in a stump overnight. In the morning it's never quite where I left it. I've stopped marking the place.
Keep to the planks and the road. I lost a boot off the end of this landing in May, and I've cut here twenty years.
The water's higher than it was. It doesn't rain any more than it used to. It's just higher.
I cut and stack by the hut. By morning the stack's a bundle or two lower. I've counted them in and counted them out, and nothing I know of eats reed.
If you hear somebody calling from the water, it's the herons. Mostly.
Afternoon. Rooms by the week, teas all day. Nobody's taken a room since the spring, but I keep them aired.
The lamp by the door is lit at dusk and I don't put it out. People on the road like to see a light. Things off the road don't, as far as I can tell.
Doors shut at nine. If anyone knocks after that, it isn't us they want. I don't open to find out.
Halfway between what, people ask, and point at the sign. I tell them it was halfway when it was painted.

country_man.speaker: A Man in a Grey Coat

lines: If you're out after the lamps, keep to where it's lit. I've no reason to give you. I just do it myself, and I'm still here.
You'll have come in on the Sunday train. I remember when it ran every day. Or I remember people saying it did.
Did you hear the bell last night, at nine? It was louder than usual. Everybody I've asked says it wasn't.
I'm waiting for the carrier. He comes on Tuesdays.
It isn't Tuesday. I know it isn't. I like to be early.
A woman comes to the door drying her hands. She's nothing to sell and nothing to buy, thank you, and she hopes you get where you're going before the lamps.
"Who is it?" A man's voice, then: "No, thank you. We keep early hours out here."
The door is locked. Through the window: a table laid for four, and three chairs.
A voice says, not unkindly, that they don't open to people off the road. "Is it still light out? Then you've time to get on."
The light inside goes out while you are still knocking.
The door gives an inch and stops. Something heavy has been pushed against it from the inside.
The doors are barred on the outside. A card is pinned to them: PLEASE DON'T LOOK IN THE BARN. THANK YOU.
Padlocked. The padlock is new and the shed is not.
THE HALFWAY HOUSE. ROOMS. TEAS. Halfway between what, the sign does not say.
There is a bench in the porch, out of the wind. If it goes badly out there, this is where you will wake.
THE HALFWAY HOUSE. ROOMS. A light behind the curtains upstairs.
The door opens before you have knocked twice. A woman in a dressing gown stands back to let you in, and does not ask your name.

options.label: Sit in the porch a while

lines: The room is at the top of the stairs. You hear nothing all night. In the morning nobody is about, the porch door is on the latch, and your tea is on the step.
You sit with your back to the door. The night does not get any shorter for it. If it goes badly out there, this is where you will wake.
A bucket on a chain. The water at the bottom is further down than the chain is long.
A candle in a box on a post. It was lit today, and nobody has passed you on this road.
EGGS. HONESTY BOX. The box is full of buttons.
Blankets, a tin plate, and a pair of good boots with nobody's feet in them.
The earth at the mouth is worn smooth. Whatever uses it goes in and out every day, and it is bigger than a rabbit.
The hive is quiet. You are meant to tell the bees when somebody dies. Nobody has told these anything for a while.
An iron pump, the green paint worn off the handle where it is held. The water comes up cold on the second stroke.
The name has worn away. The flowers on it are fresh.
The hen goes round the same few spots, always in the same order, and stands at each one a while before it moves on.
They keep to the same few yards of grass all day, though nothing is stopping them. Nobody brings them in, and by the bell they are not here.
It does not run from you. As far as you can see, it does not run from anything.
